text.title: C4 Drift Detection from IaC — Worked Examples
text.summary: One complete post-apply drift report for an orders platform on Terraform, with a note on every value a reader might question, and one report from the same system as first scripted that breaks six subject rules and what the validator and the architect on rotation say about it.

section.title: Scenario
section.p: The orders platform keeps a Structurizr DSL model in `docs/c4/` and runs on Terraform in `orders-prod`. The first drift script parsed `.tf` files, skipped IAM roles with a `continue` statement, and reported "the diagram is a bit out of date". The architect on rotation runs steps 1-8 of `content/04-procedure.xml`; the post-apply run after Thursday's apply produces the report below.

section.title: Good example: post-apply report at state serial 412

example.title: Three findings, one unmapped type, one escalation
example.note: `iac_state.identity` carries the Terraform serial 412 and the lineage: with the model commit `3f9a2c1d` beside it, a reader can tell whether the model is behind or the state moved since the report.
`drift-0041` is `added` with `c4_element_id` prefixed `expected:` because the DLQ has no element yet; its closure is the model commit `8b1e4d7a` that adds one, made the same afternoon.

`drift-0042` is the `edge-changed` class the rule exists for: a security-group rule now lets the API reach the ledger database directly, which nobody drew. It is `open` and will be escalated if it survives the next report.
`drift-0037` is `accepted` with a reason and an expiry inside one cadence, and because it has been open for two reports it appears in `escalated_finding_ids` and in the header.

`allowlist.suppressed` prints a count per entry (76 resources in total) and `hardcoded_skips_in_script` is false: the IAM role `continue` that used to live in the script is now an allowlist entry with the number 22 next to it.
`reconciliation` is 76 + 54 + 1 = 131; the one unmapped `aws_msk_serverless_cluster` will be added to the mapping table in this review rather than dropped.

section.title: Bad example: the first script's report

example.title: Six subject rules broken
example.note: What the validator prints: `c4_model.format: 'png' not in allowed enum` (r-c4-model-machine-readable); `iac_state.identity: missing required field: serial` and `lineage` (r-compare-applied-state-not-source, r-run-on-apply-and-on-schedule); `allowlist.hardcoded_skips_in_script: True is not the required const False` (r-noise-allowlist-explicit); `run.post_apply_hook_wired: False` (r-run-on-apply-and-on-schedule); `findings[0].closure: missing required field: commit` on a model-commit closure and `findings[1].closure: missing required field: expires_on` with reason "known, ignore" under minLength (r-finding-closes-by-commit-or-expiry); `findings[2].class: 'diagram-stale' not in allowed enum` and `iac_address` / `c4_element_id` under minLength (r-three-drift-classes-with-ids).

What the architect sees beyond the validator: `reconciliation` says 0 allowlisted and 54 mapped out of 131, so 77 resources vanished between state and report; `drift-0037` has been open three reports and is not escalated; and the report is scheduled only, so Thursday's apply would have gone unreported until Monday. The report goes back to step 1.

list.item: Two identities, not one: the model commit and the state serial are what separate "update the diagram" from "someone changed production by hand".
The suppressed count is the allowlist's honesty check; a skip in code has no count and therefore no reviewer.
An expiry date is what turns "known" into a question that gets asked again on a schedule.
